reply.english: And upon you too, God keep you
And blessed Eid to you too

phrases.arabic: وينكن؟ ليش ما إجيتو تعيّدو معنا؟

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: عيد مبارك يا أم أحمد!
dialogue.english: Blessed Eid, Umm Ahmad!

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: الله يبارك فيكي، كل سنة وإنتي طيبة
dialogue.transliteration: allah ybaarek fiiki, kell sene w-ente tayybe
dialogue.english: God bless you, may you be well every year

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: ينعاد عليكي
dialogue.english: May you witness it again next year

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: الله يخلّيكي، تفضّلي إدخلي
dialogue.english: God keep you, please come in

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: شكراً، شو ريحة المعمول هيدي؟
dialogue.english: Thanks, what is that smell of ma'mool?

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: عملنا معمول وكعك من مبارح
dialogue.english: We made ma'mool and cookies since yesterday

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: يعطيكي العافية، بدّي واحدة!
dialogue.english: God give you strength, I want one!

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: تكرمي، خدي قدّ ما بدّك
dialogue.english: You're welcome, take as many as you want

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: وين الولاد؟
dialogue.english: Where are the kids?

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: راحو عصلاة العيد مع أبوهن، هلّق بيرجعوا
dialogue.transliteration: raa7o 3a salaat l-3eed ma3 2abuhon, halla2 byerja3o
dialogue.english: They went to the Eid prayer with their father, they'll be back soon

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: وأنا لازم روح لعند ستّي، وعدتها إزورها بكرا الصبح
dialogue.transliteration: w-ana laazem roo7 la-3end sitti, wa3adta 2ezoorha bokra s-sob7
dialogue.english: And I have to go to my grandma's, I promised to visit her tomorrow morning

dialogue.speaker: Umm Ahmad
dialogue.arabic: الله معك، سلّمي عليها وعيدها مبارك
dialogue.english: God be with you, greet her for me and blessed Eid to her

pair.english: May you be well every year

pair.arabic: وينكن؟ ليش ما إجيتو تعيّدو معنا؟
pair.english: Where were you, why didn't you come to celebrate Eid with us?

response.english: Honestly we were busy, forgive us

lessons.culture: Among Lebanese Muslims Eid starts with the prayer in the morning, then families visit each other, elders first, and the host puts out ma'mool, cookies and sweets. Children are given "عيدية" (a little money) by the grown-ups.

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "عيد مبارك". Reply naturally.

too_formal.item: تقبّل الله منّا ومنكم صالح الأعمال
too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a long religious formula from sermons; everyday Lebanese speech says "الله يبارك فيك".

exercises.tip: Add "فيكي" for a woman and "فيكن" for several people.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "كل سنة وإنتو ____". Meaning: May you be well every year.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "عام" and "أنتم" are formal; Lebanese says "سنة" and "إنتو".

exercises.tip: "طيبين" here means "in good health and spirits".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Blessed Eid to you all."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is written-style; the everyday greeting is short.

exercises.tip: "-كن" on the end means "you all" in Lebanese.

exercises.prompt: What is the money children get from adults at Eid called?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "هبة" is a bookish word nobody says on the street.

exercises.tip: The "عيدية" is normally money, not an object.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "We're going to the Eid prayer."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "ذاهبون" is formal; everyday speech says "رايحين".

exercises.tip: "عصلاة" is the spoken squeeze of "على صلاة".

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "ينعاد عليكن". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a long formula; a short blessing is what people actually say.

exercises.tip: "وعليكن" hands the same wish back to them.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عم ____ تياب العيد". Meaning: I'm putting on my Eid clothes.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "أرتدي" is formal; Lebanese says "بلبس".

exercises.tip: "عم" + "بـ" shows it is happening right now: "عم بلبس".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "We visited grandma today."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "جدّتنا" is the formal word; families say "ستّي" or "تيتا".

exercises.tip: "ستّي" and "تيتا" both mean grandma in Lebanon.

exercises.prompt: Which sweet is typical for Eid?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a general phrase, not the name of a sweet.

exercises.tip: Ma'mool is filled with dates, walnuts or pistachios.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "Blessed Eid to you all."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is another formal greeting, not the phrase asked for.

exercises.tip: The order is: the thing (Eid), then the blessing.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: رمضان كريم يا نادية!
dialogue.english: Ramadan kareem, Nadia!

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: الله أكرم، كيفك يا رامي؟
dialogue.english: God is more generous, how are you, Rami?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: تمام الحمدلله، بس جوعان شوي، بلّشنا نصوم من الفجر
dialogue.transliteration: tamaam l-7amdella, bass joo3aan shwayy, ballashna nsoom mn el-fajr
dialogue.english: Fine thank God, just a bit hungry, we started fasting at dawn

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: الله يعينك، الساعة قدّيش الإفطار اليوم؟
dialogue.english: God help you, what time is iftar today?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: عالسبعة إلا ربع، بيضرب المدفع
dialogue.english: At quarter to seven, the cannon fires

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: نحنا عم نحضّر للإفطار من الصبح
dialogue.english: We've been preparing for iftar since the morning

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: شو عملتو؟
dialogue.english: What did you make?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: فتّوش وشوربة عدس، وعملنا قطايف للحلو
dialogue.english: Fattoush and lentil soup, and we made qatayef for dessert

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: يعطيكي العافية، الله يتقبّل صيامك
dialogue.english: God give you strength, may God accept your fasting

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: منّا ومنّك يا رب. وإنت عند مين معزوم الليلة؟
dialogue.transliteration: minna w minnak ya rabb. w-ente 3end meen ma3zoom l-leyle?
dialogue.english: From us and from you. And you, whose invitation are you going to tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.arabic: عند أهل مرتي، وبعد الفطور منسهر شوي
dialogue.transliteration: 3end ahl marti, w ba3d l-ftoor mensaher shwayy
dialogue.english: At my wife's family, and after iftar we'll stay up a while

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: الله يهنّيكن، الله يجمعنا بخير
dialogue.english: God make it a happy time for you, may God bring us together in good

pair.english: Whose iftar are you invited to tonight?

lessons.culture: In Ramadan Lebanese Muslim families gather for iftar every evening with dishes like fattoush and lentil soup, and sweets such as qatayef come after. In some old neighbourhoods a "مسحّراتي" still wakes people for suhoor, and a cannon or the call to prayer marks the moment to break the fast.

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "رمضان كريم". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a bookish wish; the answer everyone gives is "الله أكرم".

exercises.tip: It is a fixed pair: "رمضان كريم" then "الله أكرم".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "رمضان ____". Meaning: Ramadan is generous.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal welcome; the everyday greeting is short.

exercises.tip: Both "كريم" and "مبارك" are said, with different replies.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "We're fasting."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "صائمون" is formal; Lebanese says "صايمين" and "نحنا".

exercises.tip: "نحنا" is the Lebanese "we".

exercises.prompt: What is the meal before dawn called?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a descriptive phrase, not the name.

exercises.tip: "السحور" is eaten before the dawn prayer; "الإفطار" is at sunset.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "What time is iftar today?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "متى" is formal; Lebanese asks with "الساعة قدّيش" or "إيمتى".

exercises.tip: "قدّيش" is "how much", so "الساعة قدّيش" is "what time".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "الساعة قدّيش الإفطار اليوم؟" Say it is at quarter to seven.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it sounds like a train announcement.

exercises.tip: "إلا ربع" means "minus a quarter".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "عند مين ____ عالإفطار الليلة؟". Meaning: Whose invitation are you going to tonight?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "مدعو" is written style; "معزوم" is what people say.

exercises.tip: "معزومة" for a woman, "معزومين" for several people.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "May God accept your fasting."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is the written past-tense wish; speech uses "الله يتقبّل".

exercises.tip: The usual reply is "منّا ومنّك".

exercises.prompt: Which one is a stuffed sweet pastry typical of Ramadan?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a category, not the name of a sweet.

exercises.tip: Qatayef are folded pancakes filled with cream or nuts.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "We're preparing for iftar."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal phrase.

exercises.tip: "عم" then the verb shows it is happening now.

phrases.arabic: زينة منصّة العريس والعروس كتير حلوة

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: مبروك يا كريم! سمعت إنّو خيّك عم يتجوّز
dialogue.transliteration: mabrouk ya Kariim! sme3et 2enno khayyak 3am yetjawwaz
dialogue.english: Congratulations Karim! I heard your brother is getting married

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: الله يبارك فيكي، إي، العرس بعد إسبوعين
dialogue.transliteration: allah ybaarek fiiki, ee, l-3ars ba3d 2esboo3ayn
dialogue.english: God bless you, yes, the wedding is in two weeks

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: إيمتى بالضبط؟
dialogue.english: When exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: يوم السبت الجاي، وإنتي وعيلتك معزومين
dialogue.transliteration: yoom es-sabt l-jaay, w-ente w 3eeltek ma3zumiin
dialogue.english: Next Saturday, and you and your family are invited

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: الله يسعدهن! وين العرس؟
dialogue.english: God make them happy! Where is the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: بصالة كبيرة بجونية، والكل عم يحضّر
dialogue.english: In a big hall in Jounieh, and everyone is preparing

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: عم يحضّروا للعرس من زمان، صح؟
dialogue.english: They've been preparing for the wedding for ages, right?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: إي، والعروس اختارِت فستان أبيض كتير حلو، وزينة المنصّة كمان
dialogue.transliteration: ee, wel-3aroos 2ikhtaaret fostaan 2abyad ktiir 7elo, w zeenet l-manassa kamaan
dialogue.english: Yes, and the bride chose a very beautiful white dress, and the stage decoration too

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: إن شاء الله بتكون زفّة حلوة ودبكة كمان!
dialogue.transliteration: 2in shaa2 allah bet-kuun zaffe 7elwe w dabke kamaan!
dialogue.english: God willing there'll be a nice procession and dabke too!

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، أول ما توصل الزفّة بتبلّش الدبكة
dialogue.english: Of course, as soon as the procession arrives the dabke starts

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: وإنت شو جبتلن هدية؟
dialogue.english: And you, what gift did you bring them?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: جبتلن غرض للبيت، وعقبالك يا ليلى
dialogue.transliteration: jibtelon gharad lel-beit, w 3o2baalek ya Layla
dialogue.english: I got them something for the house, and may it be your turn, Layla

pair.english: May it be your turn next

lessons.culture: Lebanese weddings are big and loud: the "زفّة" (procession with drums) opens the party and the dabke follows. Guests bring a gift or money in an envelope, and "عقبالك" is said warmly to single guests.

exercises.prompt: At a wedding a friend says to you: "عقبالك!". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is stiff; a short reply is normal.

exercises.tip: "يا رب" or "إن شاء الله" are also fine.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "____ العرس". Meaning: Congratulations on the wedding.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal wedding blessing, not the everyday word.

exercises.tip: "مبروك" works for every happy news.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "When is their wedding?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "متى" and "زفاف" are formal; Lebanese says "إيمتى" and "عرس".

exercises.tip: "-ن" on "عرسن" means "their".

exercises.prompt: What is the wedding procession with drums called?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is the written term.

exercises.tip: The "زفّة" brings the couple in with drums and singing.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "The wedding procession is coming."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a news-reader style sentence.

exercises.tip: "جاية" is feminine because "الزفّة" is feminine.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "مين معزوم عالعرس؟" Say: the whole family and friends.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is formal.

exercises.tip: "العيلة" is the Lebanese word for family.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "شو جبتلن ____؟". Meaning: What gift did you bring them?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal full sentence.

exercises.tip: "جبتلن" = "جبت" (I brought) + "لن" (for them).

exercises.prompt: Translate: "She wore a white dress."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "ارتدت" and "ثوب" are formal here.

exercises.tip: "لبسِت" is "she wore"; "لبست" is also "I wore".

exercises.prompt: Which folk dance starts at Lebanese weddings?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a general phrase.

exercises.tip: The dabke is danced in a line, holding hands.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "The dabke started."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "بدأت" is formal; speech says "بلّشِت".

exercises.tip: "بلّش" is the everyday verb for "start".

reply.english: God bless you, come and visit us

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: كل سنة وإنتي طيّبة يا مايا!
dialogue.transliteration: kell sene w-ente tayybe ya Maaya!
dialogue.english: Happy birthday, Maya!

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: وإنت طيّب، الله يخلّيك
dialogue.english: And you too, God keep you

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: قدّيش صار عمرك هالسنة؟
dialogue.english: How old did you turn this year?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: صرت تلاتين، يا ويلي!
dialogue.english: I turned thirty, oh dear!

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: ما شاء الله، شو بدّك هدية؟
dialogue.transliteration: maa shaa2 allah, shoo beddek hediyye?
dialogue.english: Masha'Allah, what gift do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: ولا شي، بس تجي عالحفلة
dialogue.english: Nothing, just come to the party

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، إيمتى الحفلة؟
dialogue.english: Of course, when is the party?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: بكرا بالليل، وإمّي عم تحضّر الكاتو
dialogue.english: Tomorrow night, and my mother is preparing the cake

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: الله يعطيها العافية، وبدّي شوفك عم تطفّي الشمعات
dialogue.transliteration: allah ye3tiiha l-3aafye, w beddi shoofek 3am tetaffi sh-sham3aat
dialogue.english: God give her strength, and I want to see you blow out the candles

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: إي، وبتاكل كاتو معنا كمان
dialogue.transliteration: ee, w bta2kol kaatoo ma3na kamaan
dialogue.english: Yes, and you'll eat cake with us too

dialogue.speaker: Hadi
dialogue.arabic: وسمعت إنّو خيّك صار عنده مولود، مبروك!
dialogue.transliteration: w sme3et 2enno khayyek saar 3endo mawlood, mabrouk!
dialogue.english: And I heard your brother had a baby, congratulations!

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.arabic: الله يبارك فيك، الله يطوّل عمرك
dialogue.english: God bless you, may God lengthen your life

response.english: Nothing, just come to the party

lessons.culture: Lebanese wish a birthday with "كل سنة وإنت طيّب", and many also say the English "happy birthday". A new baby is welcomed with visits, gifts and a bowl of meghli, and people go to see a new house with a gift.

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "كل سنة وإنت طيّب". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "بخير" is formal; "طيّب" is what people say.

exercises.tip: Use "طيّبة" if you are speaking to a woman.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "كل سنة وإنت ____". Meaning: Happy birthday.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "عام" and "أنت" are formal.

exercises.tip: "طيّب" here means "well".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Congratulations on the new house."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "المسكن" is a formal word for house.

exercises.tip: The order is: "مبروك", the thing, then its description.

exercises.prompt: What do you say to wish someone a long life?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is an old-fashioned phrase.

exercises.tip: It is said on many occasions, not only birthdays.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "Blow out the candles."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "أطفئ" is formal; speech says "طفّي".

exercises.tip: "طفّي" is also "turn off" for a light.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "قدّيش صار عمرك؟" Say you turned thirty.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "بلغت" is formal.

exercises.tip: "صرت" is "I became", which is how you give your age.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "شو بدّك ____؟". Meaning: What gift do you want?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal sentence.

exercises.tip: "بدّك" is "you want" in Lebanese.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "We're preparing the cake."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "الكعكة" is the formal word for a cake.

exercises.tip: Lebanese says "كاتو" (from French) or "تورتة".

exercises.prompt: What do many Lebanese call a birthday cake?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but "كعكة" is the formal word.

exercises.tip: "كاتو" comes from the French "gâteau".

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "Congratulations on the promotion."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but it is a formal sentence.

exercises.tip: "مبروك" comes first.

challenge.title: Congratulate a friend
challenge.instructions: Pick an occasion (Eid, Ramadan, a wedding or a birthday) and write a short Lebanese conversation of at least 8 lines in which you congratulate a friend and they answer. Say it aloud too.
required_elements: A greeting or congratulation that fits the occasion you chose
A natural reply to the congratulation, such as الله يبارك فيك
A question about the details (when, where or who), using إيمتى, وين or مين
A wish or blessing such as عقبالك, الله يخلّيك or الله يطوّل عمرك

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.arabic: مبروك يا أبو ليث، سمعت إنّو البيت الجديد جاهز!

dialogue.speaker: Abu Leith
dialogue.arabic: الله يبارك فيك يا خالد

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.arabic: مبروك البيت الجديد، وينو بالضبط؟

dialogue.speaker: Abu Leith
dialogue.arabic: بالحازميّة، قريب من أهلي

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.arabic: الله يخلّيه إلك، وإيمتى بتعمل حفلة؟
dialogue.english: May God keep it for you, and when are you having a party?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Leith
dialogue.arabic: السبت الجاي، وإنت معزوم إنت وعيلتك
dialogue.english: Next Saturday, you and your family are invited

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.arabic: الله يطوّل عمرك، وعقبال عندي كمان
dialogue.english: May God lengthen your life, and may it be my turn too

dialogue.speaker: Abu Leith
dialogue.arabic: يا رب من عندك يا خالد
dialogue.english: God willing, Khaled
